\section{Introduction}
Neural-network training couples nonlinear function approximation to optimization in a high-dimensional parameter space. The neural tangent kernel viewpoint reorganizes this complexity around a matrix of parameter sensitivities. For each training example, the model Jacobian supplies a vector whose coordinates describe infinitesimal response to each parameter. Inner products of these vectors form a Gram matrix, which describes both similarity of local responses and the projection of parameter gradients back to prediction space.

The statement that wide-network gradient descent approaches kernel regression combines several logically distinct components: Gram positivity; an exact linearized kernel action; contraction under a suitable spectrum and learning rate; limited kernel drift along training; and, in architecture-specific settings, concentration around a deterministic infinite-width limit. This paper gives a self-contained deterministic account of the first four components. It does not infer strict convergence from positive semidefiniteness alone: null directions and oversized learning rates are real obstructions.

Our results consist of an exact energy identity, an exact residual trajectory for fixed-kernel training, a geometric error theorem under one-step contraction, and an explicit entrywise perturbation estimate. Together they provide an interface into which probabilistic concentration and width scaling can be inserted.

\section{Finite-sample setting}
Let $n,p\in\mathbb N$. Predictions, targets, and residuals on the sample are vectors in $\R^n$.

\begin{definition}[Pairing and squared norm]
For $u,v\in\R^n$, set
\[
\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^n u_iv_i,
\qquad \norm{u}_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^n u_i^2.
\]
The squared norm is nonnegative because it is a sum of squares.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sample Jacobian and NTK]
A sample Jacobian is $J\in\R^{n\times p}$, where $J_{ia}$ is the local response of prediction $i$ to parameter $a$. Its neural tangent kernel is
\[
K_{ik}=\sum_{a=1}^p J_{ia}J_{ka},
\qquad K=JJ^{\mathsf T}.
\]
For $v\in\R^n$, $(Kv)_i=\sum_{k=1}^nK_{ik}v_k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Residual-induced parameter gradient]
For $r\in\R^n$, define $g\in\R^p$ by
\[
g_a=\sum_{i=1}^nJ_{ia}r_i,
\qquad g=J^{\mathsf T}r.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fixed-kernel training]
Given target $y$, initial prediction $f_0$, kernel $K$, and learning rate $\eta$, define
\[
f_{t+1}=f_t+\eta K(y-f_t).
\]
Let $r_t=y-f_t$ and define $R_{K,\eta}(v)=v-\eta Kv=(I-\eta K)v$.
\end{definition}

\section{Gram geometry}
\begin{theorem}[Symmetry]
For every sample Jacobian, $K_{ik}=K_{ki}$ for all $i,k$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Commutativity gives
$K_{ik}=\sum_aJ_{ia}J_{ka}=\sum_aJ_{ka}J_{ia}=K_{ki}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Kernel energy identity]
For every $r\in\R^n$, with $g=J^{\mathsf T}r$,
\[
\langle r,Kr\rangle=\sum_{a=1}^p g_a^2=\norm{J^{\mathsf T}r}_2^2.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Expanding and reordering finite sums yields
\begin{align*}
r^{\mathsf T}Kr
&=\sum_i r_i\sum_k\sum_aJ_{ia}J_{ka}r_k\\
&=\sum_a\left(\sum_iJ_{ia}r_i\right)
          \left(\sum_kJ_{ka}r_k\right)
=\sum_a g_a^2.
\end{align*}
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Positive semidefiniteness]
Every NTK satisfies $r^{\mathsf T}Kr\geq0$ for every $r\in\R^n$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The energy identity expresses the quadratic form as a sum of squares.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Null directions]
The energy vanishes exactly when $J^{\mathsf T}r=0$. Hence positive semidefiniteness need not mean positive definiteness. A residual in $\ker(J^{\mathsf T})=\ker(K)$ is invisible to all local parameter directions represented by $J$.
\end{remark}

\section{Eliminating parameter space}
\begin{theorem}[Jacobian--kernel correspondence]
If $g=J^{\mathsf T}r$, then the linearized prediction change is $Jg=Kr$; componentwise,
\[
\sum_{a=1}^pJ_{ia}g_a=(Kr)_i.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Substitution and exchange of sums give
\[
\sum_aJ_{ia}\sum_kJ_{ka}r_k
=\sum_k\left(\sum_aJ_{ia}J_{ka}\right)r_k
=\sum_kK_{ik}r_k.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Residual recurrence]
Fixed-kernel training satisfies
\[
r_{t+1}=R_{K,\eta}(r_t)=(I-\eta K)r_t.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Since $r_t=y-f_t$,
$r_{t+1}=y-f_t-\eta K(y-f_t)=r_t-\eta Kr_t$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact trajectory]
For every $t\in\mathbb N$,
\[
r_t=R_{K,\eta}^{\,t}(r_0)=(I-\eta K)^t(y-f_0).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The case $t=0$ is immediate. If the formula holds at $t$, the recurrence gives
$ r_{t+1}=R_{K,\eta}(R_{K,\eta}^{\,t}(r_0))=R_{K,\eta}^{\,t+1}(r_0)$.
Induction proves the statement.
\end{proof}

\section{Geometric convergence}
\begin{theorem}[Uniform contraction implies geometric decay]
Let $q\geq0$ and suppose
\[
\norm{R_{K,\eta}(v)}_2^2\leq q\norm{v}_2^2
\quad\text{for every }v\in\R^n.
\]
Then for every $s_0\in\R^n$ and $t\in\mathbb N$,
\[
\norm{R_{K,\eta}^{\,t}(s_0)}_2^2
\leq q^t\norm{s_0}_2^2.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At $t=0$ there is equality. Assuming the bound at $t$, the one-step hypothesis and $q\geq0$ imply
\begin{align*}
\norm{R^{t+1}(s_0)}_2^2
&\leq q\norm{R^t(s_0)}_2^2
\leq q(q^t\norm{s_0}_2^2)
=q^{t+1}\norm{s_0}_2^2.
\end{align*}
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Geometric convergence of fixed-NTK training]
Let $K=JJ^{\mathsf T}$. Under the contraction hypothesis above,
\[
\norm{y-f_t}_2^2\leq q^t\norm{y-f_0}_2^2.
\]
If $q<1$, the residual converges to zero.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Combine the exact trajectory with the contraction theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Spectral sufficient condition]
Suppose the eigenvalues of symmetric $K$ lie in $[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}]$ with $0<\lambda_{\min}\leq\lambda_{\max}$. If $0<\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}$, then contraction holds with
\[
q=\max_{\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(K)}|1-\eta\lambda|^2<1.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In an orthonormal eigenbasis, $I-\eta K$ multiplies the $\lambda$-eigenmode by $1-\eta\lambda$. The squared norm is bounded by the largest squared multiplier. The step-size interval places every multiplier strictly between $-1$ and $1$.
\end{proof}

If $K$ has a zero eigenvalue, the corresponding multiplier equals $1$; if $\eta\lambda>2$, its magnitude exceeds $1$. Gram positivity is therefore distinct from strict contraction.

\section{Quantitative kernel stability}
\begin{theorem}[Entrywise stability under Jacobian perturbation]
Let $J^{(0)},J^{(1)}\in\R^{n\times p}$ and $B\geq0$. Assume, for every $i,a$,
\[
|J^{(0)}_{ia}|\leq B,\quad |J^{(1)}_{ia}|\leq B,
\quad |J^{(1)}_{ia}-J^{(0)}_{ia}|\leq\delta.
\]
For $K^{(s)}=J^{(s)}(J^{(s)})^{\mathsf T}$,
\[
|K^{(1)}_{ik}-K^{(0)}_{ik}|\leq2pB\delta
\]
for every $i,k$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each parameter coordinate,
\begin{align*}
J^{(1)}_{ia}J^{(1)}_{ka}-J^{(0)}_{ia}J^{(0)}_{ka}
={}&J^{(1)}_{ia}(J^{(1)}_{ka}-J^{(0)}_{ka})\\
&+J^{(0)}_{ka}(J^{(1)}_{ia}-J^{(0)}_{ia}).
\end{align*}
The absolute value is at most $B\delta+B\delta=2B\delta$. Sum over $p$ coordinates and use the triangle inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Near constancy along a bounded path]
Let $J(\theta)\in\R^{n\times p}$ depend on $\theta\in\R$, and fix $\theta_0$. Suppose $B,L\geq0$,
\[
|J(\theta)_{ia}|\leq B,
\qquad
|J(\theta)_{ia}-J(\theta_0)_{ia}|\leq L|\theta-\theta_0|.
\]
If $|\theta_t-\theta_0|\leq t\eta G$, then
\[
|K(\theta_t)_{ik}-K(\theta_0)_{ik}|\leq2pBLt\eta G
\]
for all $i,k$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The path and Lipschitz bounds give entrywise Jacobian drift at most $Lt\eta G$. Apply the preceding theorem with $\delta=Lt\eta G$.
\end{proof}

The factor $p$ exposes the unnormalized coordinate count. In wide-network parameterizations, $B$ and $\delta$ generally depend on width, so the controlling quantity is $pB\delta$. The pathwise estimate is most useful on horizons for which $t\eta G$ remains controlled.

\section{Algorithms and complexity}
\paragraph{Empirical kernel construction.}
Compute $K=JJ^{\mathsf T}$. Direct construction takes $O(n^2p)$ arithmetic and $O(n^2)$ storage. If only $Kv$ is needed, compute $J(J^{\mathsf T}v)$ in $O(np)$ time without storing $K$.

\paragraph{Fixed-kernel residual descent.}
Initialize $r_0=y-f_0$ and repeat $r_{t+1}=r_t-\eta Kr_t$, recovering $f_{t+1}=y-r_{t+1}$. A dense iteration costs $O(n^2)$; an implicit Jacobian product costs $O(np)$.

\paragraph{Kernel-drift certificate.}
Compute
\[
B=\max_{i,a}\max\{|J^{(0)}_{ia}|,|J^{(1)}_{ia}|\},\qquad
\delta=\max_{i,a}|J^{(1)}_{ia}-J^{(0)}_{ia}|.
\]
Then $2pB\delta$ certifies every entry. Computing $B,\delta$ costs $O(np)$; constructing both dense kernels for comparison costs $O(n^2p)$.

\section{Numerical illustrations}
Take
\[
J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
K=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&2&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This kernel is symmetric positive semidefinite but singular because $J$ has two columns and three rows. A null residual does not decay.

For strict contraction, take $J=\operatorname{diag}(1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$, so $K=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,3)$. With $\eta=1/2$, residual multipliers are $1/2,0,-1/2$, and $q=1/4$. Hence
\[
\norm{r_t}_2^2\leq4^{-t}\norm{r_0}_2^2.
\]
For stability, if $p=100$, $B=1.2$, and $\delta=10^{-4}$, every kernel entry changes by at most $2pB\delta=0.024$.

\section{Perturbed and time-varying dynamics}
Let $K_t$ be the kernel at time $t$ and $K_0$ a reference kernel. The residual step decomposes as
\[
r_{t+1}=(I-\eta K_0)r_t-\eta(K_t-K_0)r_t.
\]
The first term is the reference dynamics and the second is forcing caused by drift. If every entry of $K_t-K_0$ is bounded by $\varepsilon_t$, then
\[
\norm{(K_t-K_0)v}_2\leq n\varepsilon_t\norm{v}_2.
\]
Indeed, every output coordinate is at most $\varepsilon_t\sum_j|v_j|\leq\varepsilon_t\sqrt n\norm{v}_2$ in magnitude, and summing $n$ coordinate squares proves the estimate. The pathwise certificate therefore implies
\[
\norm{K_t-K_0}_{2\to2}\leq2npBLt\eta G.
\]
This conversion is conservative because it allows all worst-case entry deviations to align.

If $\norm{(I-\eta K_0)v}_2\leq\rho\norm{v}_2$ with $0\leq\rho<1$ and $\norm{K_t-K_0}_{2\to2}\leq\varepsilon$, then the triangle inequality gives
\[
\norm{r_{t+1}}_2\leq(\rho+|\eta|\varepsilon)\norm{r_t}_2.
\]
Thus the changing-kernel step remains contractive whenever $\rho+|\eta|\varepsilon<1$. The spectral margin of the reference dynamics quantifies its tolerance to kernel drift.

A practical analysis accordingly has four stages: construct the sample Gram kernel; estimate its nonzero spectrum and choose a stable learning rate; monitor Jacobian magnitude and drift; and compare the perturbation with the contraction margin. This distinguishes nullspace obstruction, unstable step size, and excessive feature drift, which require different remedies.

\section{Applications and limitations}
If the Jacobian remains close to initialization, prediction updates remain close to those generated by the initial kernel. If that kernel concentrates around a deterministic limit as width increases, the network trajectory can approach deterministic kernel descent. The deterministic interfaces needed are an initialization concentration estimate, pathwise Jacobian drift, and perturbation control transferring contraction from the limit to the empirical time-varying kernel.

The image of $J$ is the space of available linearized prediction changes. The kernel has the same image; its nullspace contains unreachable residual patterns. Eigenvalues diagnose learning rates and slow modes, while preconditioning aims to compress the nonzero spectral range. Kernel drift distinguishes nearly frozen sensitivity features from order-one feature learning.

The present theory is finite-sample and deterministic. It does not establish concentration for a particular random architecture. Its path is scalar, and its stability result is entrywise rather than spectral. In singular problems, global contraction may fail even though contraction holds on the Jacobian image or on the subspace reached from a particular initial residual.

\section{Future directions}
Promising extensions include uniform operator-norm concentration over a training horizon; width-dependent $O(m^{-1/2})$ tracking of kernel regression up to logarithmic factors; a scaling threshold separating lazy dynamics from feature learning; preconditioning on the low-rank Jacobian image; and adaptive learning rates based on online estimates of extremal kernel eigenvalues.

\section{Conclusion}
The sample Jacobian induces a symmetric positive semidefinite Gram kernel. A residual-induced parameter gradient changes linearized predictions by exactly this kernel. Fixed-kernel training therefore obeys an exact residual recurrence; a one-step contraction gives a geometric finite-time rate. Entrywise Jacobian control gives an explicit kernel-drift estimate, and Lipschitz control along a short learning-rate-scaled path makes near constancy quantitative.

The separation is essential. Gram positivity is automatic, but strict contraction is spectral. Fixed-kernel dynamics are exact for the kernel iteration, but their relevance to nonlinear training depends on Jacobian stability. Infinite width enters through concentration and normalization, not through the underlying finite-dimensional algebra.

"""Numerical demonstrations of finite-sample neural tangent kernel dynamics.

The script uses only the Python standard library.  It constructs Gram kernels,
checks the energy identity, runs fixed-kernel residual descent, and evaluates the
entrywise Jacobian-drift certificate.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from math import sqrt
from typing import Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = List[float]
Matrix = List[List[float]]


def transpose(a: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> Matrix:
    """Return the transpose of a rectangular matrix."""
    if not a:
        return []
    return [list(column) for column in zip(*a)]


def matvec(a: Sequence[Sequence[float]], x: Sequence[float]) -> Vector:
    """Multiply a dense matrix by a vector."""
    if any(len(row) != len(x) for row in a):
        raise ValueError("matrix and vector dimensions do not match")
    return [sum(value * coordinate for value, coordinate in zip(row, x)) for row in a]


def matmul(a: Sequence[Sequence[float]], b: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> Matrix:
    """Multiply two dense matrices."""
    bt = transpose(b)
    if a and b and len(a[0]) != len(b):
        raise ValueError("matrix dimensions do not match")
    return [[sum(x * y for x, y in zip(row, column)) for column in bt] for row in a]


def dot(x: Sequence[float], y: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Compute the Euclidean inner product."""
    if len(x) != len(y):
        raise ValueError("vector dimensions do not match")
    return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(x, y))


def squared_norm(x: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Compute the squared Euclidean norm."""
    return dot(x, x)


def neural_tangent_kernel(jacobian: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> Matrix:
    """Construct K = J J^T from sample-by-parameter Jacobian rows."""
    return matmul(jacobian, transpose(jacobian))


def parameter_gradient(jacobian: Sequence[Sequence[float]], residual: Sequence[float]) -> Vector:
    """Compute J^T r."""
    return matvec(transpose(jacobian), residual)


def residual_descent(
    kernel: Sequence[Sequence[float]],
    learning_rate: float,
    initial_residual: Sequence[float],
    steps: int,
) -> List[Vector]:
    """Return r_0,...,r_steps for r_(t+1) = r_t - eta K r_t."""
    if steps < 0:
        raise ValueError("steps must be nonnegative")
    history = [list(initial_residual)]
    for _ in range(steps):
        kr = matvec(kernel, history[-1])
        history.append([r - learning_rate * update for r, update in zip(history[-1], kr)])
    return history


def entrywise_drift_certificate(
    jacobian_0: Sequence[Sequence[float]], jacobian_1: Sequence[Sequence[float]]
) -> Tuple[float, float, float, float]:
    """Return (B, delta, observed kernel drift, theorem bound 2 p B delta)."""
    if len(jacobian_0) != len(jacobian_1) or any(
        len(row_0) != len(row_1) for row_0, row_1 in zip(jacobian_0, jacobian_1)
    ):
        raise ValueError("Jacobians must have equal shapes")
    p = len(jacobian_0[0]) if jacobian_0 else 0
    entries_0 = [abs(x) for row in jacobian_0 for x in row]
    entries_1 = [abs(x) for row in jacobian_1 for x in row]
    differences = [
        abs(x_1 - x_0)
        for row_0, row_1 in zip(jacobian_0, jacobian_1)
        for x_0, x_1 in zip(row_0, row_1)
    ]
    b = max(entries_0 + entries_1, default=0.0)
    delta = max(differences, default=0.0)
    k0 = neural_tangent_kernel(jacobian_0)
    k1 = neural_tangent_kernel(jacobian_1)
    observed = max(
        (abs(y - x) for row_0, row_1 in zip(k0, k1) for x, y in zip(row_0, row_1)),
        default=0.0,
    )
    return b, delta, observed, 2.0 * p * b * delta


def print_matrix(name: str, matrix: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> None:
    """Pretty-print a small dense matrix."""
    print(f"{name} =")
    for row in matrix:
        print("  [" + ", ".join(f"{value:9.5f}" for value in row) + "]")


def demonstrate_energy_identity() -> None:
    """Show r^T K r = ||J^T r||^2 and Gram positivity numerically."""
    jacobian = [[1.0, -0.5, 0.2], [0.3, 1.1, -0.4], [-0.7, 0.2, 0.9]]
    residual = [1.2, -0.8, 0.5]
    kernel = neural_tangent_kernel(jacobian)
    gradient = parameter_gradient(jacobian, residual)
    left = dot(residual, matvec(kernel, residual))
    right = squared_norm(gradient)
    print("\n1. Gram energy identity")
    print_matrix("K", kernel)
    print(f"r^T K r       = {left:.12f}")
    print(f"||J^T r||^2   = {right:.12f}")
    print(f"absolute gap  = {abs(left - right):.3e}")

Vector = List[float]
Matrix = List[List[float]]


def transpose(a: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> Matrix:

    if not a:

def matvec(a: Sequence[Sequence[float]], x: Sequence[float]) -> Vector:

def matmul(a: Sequence[Sequence[float]], b: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> Matrix:

def parameter_gradient(jacobian: Sequence[Sequence[float]], residual: Sequence[float]) -> Vector:

    for _ in range(steps):
        kr = matvec(kernel, history[-1])
        history.append([r - learning_rate * update for r, update in zip(history[-1], kr)])
    return history
